fullName: Coherent High-Energy X-ray Sector for In Situ Science

status2026.detail: All four branches received first light in July 2025. On the APS Beamline Commissioning Progress chart of 5 Oct 2026, 28-ID-B,C and 28-ID-F are at stage 5 ('Scientific Commissioning and Early Experiments') and 28-ID-D,E and 28-ID-G at stage 4 ('Technical Commissioning'); none is yet in stage 6 (general user program). In Jan 2026 all four were at stage 4. The Beamline Directory still lists B/C as 'Not Currently Operational' and D/E, F, G as 'Under Development', on-site access. CHEX was delivered within the APS-U project scope (project formally completed Jan 2026). The sector currently runs on interim permanent-magnet undulators (2.8 cm upstream, 3.0 cm downstream; APS insertion-device table updated 22 Sep 2026); the baseline 18.5 mm superconducting undulator pair was delayed by SCU core-reliability issues and is planned for 2026–2027 (APS Strategic Plan 2025–29). The 2025-2 proposal call (Jan 2025) already offered a 'Feature Beamlines' proposal type for CHEX. Timeline note: the Aug 2025 update projected first experiments late 2025/early 2026 and entry into the general user program late in run 2026-1 or early in run 2026-2; as of the 5 Oct 2026 chart no CHEX station has reached stage 6, so that projection has slipped.

tagline: Coherent high-energy X-rays, split four ways, watch new materials grow one atomic layer at a time inside working reactors.
summary: CHEX, the Coherent High-Energy X-ray sector at 28-ID, watches materials as they are made: oxide films stacking up in a vacuum chamber, gallium nitride crystals growing in a hot gas reactor, a battery electrode at work. Its X-rays are energetic, mostly 15,000 to 105,000 electron-volts (15–105 keV), so they pass through quartz walls, gases and liquids. A useful share of them is also coherent: their waves march in step, a bit like laser light. Coherent X-rays scatter into a grainy speckle pattern, set by where atoms, islands and defects sit, that flickers as they move. Two undulators, magnet arrays in the ring, feed four branches: one of tunable energy, and three of fixed energy that thin crystals pick off a single shared beam. Eight experiment positions let up to four teams work at once. In October 2026 CHEX is still being commissioned, on interim undulators; first experiments have begun.

whatAPSUEnables.text: Speckle needs coherent X-rays, and the coherent share of a beam shrinks as the energy rises, so the high energies that see inside reactors were starved of it. Before the upgrade roughly one 25 keV X-ray in ten thousand was coherent; to film gallium nitride growing, scientists had to drop the monochromator for a 'pink' beam (the whole undulator peak, about 1% wide in energy) and still needed 10-second frames. The upgraded ring's electron beam is about 19 times narrower and 4 times less divergent horizontally, cutting its emittance (beam size × divergence) from 3,113 to 42 pm·rad. Speckle movies should now work at a single energy and keep pace with a growing film, and crystals sharing one beam let four such experiments run at once. The key figure: about 540 times more coherent flux at 20 keV. It is a design value for an undulator tuned to 20 keV; CHEX runs on interim undulators whose measured flux is unpublished.
quantitative: Coherent flux at 20 keV (undulator optimized for 20 keV): 312 × 10¹¹ ph/s in APS-U brightness mode vs 0.6 × 10¹¹ ph/s before the upgrade; the design report quotes the gain as a factor of 540 (FDR Table 1.1).

Effective emittance: 42 pm·rad (APS-U design, brightness mode) vs 3,113 pm·rad before the upgrade. Measured: 45 pm·rad at 50 mA and as low as 28 pm·rad in round-beam mode, vs the previous record of 134 pm·rad at ESRF-EBS (APS News 2024). The 28 pm·rad round-beam figure is per plane (ε_{x} = ε_{y} = 28.7 pm·rad): the emittance is shared equally between the two planes, not lower in total.

Calculated coherent fraction at 25 keV: ≈2% (APS-U flat beam, 2.07 m permanent-magnet undulator) vs ≈0.01% (old APS, 2.4 m undulator), about 200×; at 60 keV ≈0.6% vs ≈0.002%, about 300×. This is our Gaussian-beam estimate from the APS storage-ring source parameters and FDR Table 1.1, assuming zero energy spread; indicative only.
Pre-upgrade benchmark: XPCS of GaN growth at 25.75 keV required pink beam (ΔE/E = 1.3%), giving 1.4 × 10¹² ph/s in a 4 × 16 µm spot with 10 s frames (Ju et al. 2019).
Ju et al. (2017): with APS-U, the coherent flux at 12-ID-D-type energies would approach the total flux then available; the optimum energy for coherent flux through 4 mm of fused quartz is ≈23 keV.
FDR design (superconducting-undulator source) at 28-ID-B: 6.8–37 × 10¹² ph/s at 15 keV and 4.2–11 × 10¹² ph/s at 60 keV, into foci of 0.8–9.8 µm (H) × 0.3–3.4 µm (V) FWHM (FDR Table 4.10).
Four experiments running at once from one sector (eight positions), vs a single goniometer or instrument on comparable coherent beamlines such as ESRF ID01 (PDR comparison; APS feature page).

Scaling estimate: XPCS signal-to-noise grows linearly with coherent intensity per pixel but only as the square root of frame time, so a 100× gain in coherent intensity can shorten the shortest measurable correlation time by up to ≈10⁴ at constant signal-to-noise (standard XPCS scaling; indicative).

techniques.name: X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (surface / grazing-incidence)
techniques.text: X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (XPCS) films the speckle pattern scattered from a surface and measures how fast it changes, revealing how quickly atoms, islands or domains move, even when on average nothing seems to change. For steady processes the usual measure is the intensity autocorrelation g_{2}: how much the pattern still resembles itself after a delay. Growth never stands still, so CHEX relies on two-time correlations, which compare every moment with every other and show how the motion itself evolves. Measured near the 'anti-Bragg' position, halfway between two diffraction peaks, the speckle is most sensitive to the topmost atomic layer and follows islands and steps during deposition or etching. Speckle contrast falls if the illuminated volume exceeds the coherence lengths, the energy spread is too wide or pixels are larger than the speckles; signal-to-noise grows linearly with coherent intensity per pixel but only as the square root of frame time.

techniques.name: Coherent diffraction imaging, Bragg CDI and Bragg ptychography
techniques.text: Coherent diffraction imaging records the speckle pattern around a single small crystal and lets a computer turn it back into a 3D image, with no lens. Around a Bragg peak (Bragg CDI), the reconstructed image has a phase as well as an amplitude, and the phase maps how far atoms are displaced along the scattering direction, revealing the strain inside the crystal. Bragg ptychography extends this to larger samples by scanning overlapping spots. High energy lets the beam reach crystals inside working cells and access several reflections. The geometry must resolve the speckle: with 55 µm pixels, the coherently illuminated region (the beam spot, or the crystal if smaller) may be at most about 20 × R/E µm, with R the detector distance in metres and E the energy in keV, and about half that for the twofold oversampling the reconstruction needs. The sample must also hold still to well under a micrometre.

techniques.name: In situ surface X-ray diffraction / crystal-truncation-rod scattering
techniques.text: Surface X-ray diffraction reads the top few atomic layers of a crystal. Because a crystal ends abruptly at its surface, its diffraction spreads into faint streaks between the Bragg peaks, called crystal truncation rods, whose shape encodes the surface structure. During layer-by-layer growth the intensity at the 'anti-Bragg' point, midway between two peaks, falls as a new layer half fills and recovers as it completes, once per atomic layer: an atomic-scale stopwatch. CHEX measures these rods and the diffuse scattering around them at 15–35 keV through chamber walls, and the tunable branch can add resonant contrast, setting the energy at an element's absorption edge, to tell the metal ions in a complex oxide apart.

techniques.name: High-energy X-ray diffraction
techniques.text: High-energy X-ray diffraction at 28-ID-G uses 75 or 105 keV X-rays, energetic enough to cross centimetres of many materials, to study bulk synthesis, crystal growth, corrosion and materials under mechanical or environmental load, deep inside furnaces, reactors and thick samples. At these energies the Bragg angles are small, so a flat area detector captures a wide range of reflections at once. Beryllium lenses barely bend such X-rays, so the design gives G nickel lenses, which bend them more strongly.

techniques.name: X-ray reflection interface microscopy
techniques.text: X-ray reflection interface microscopy makes a real-space image of a surface or buried interface using X-rays reflected from it. A zone plate, a microscopic pattern of concentric rings that focuses X-rays by diffraction, acts as the objective lens behind the sample, and contrast comes from how strongly each patch reflects, so atomic steps and domains show up. In the design the zone plate rides on the diffractometer's detector arm and the camera on the long-distance detector positioner. It was proposed together with Bragg coherent imaging for geochemical interfaces, such as minerals reacting with fluids.

techniques.name: Hard X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (with PLD)
techniques.text: Hard X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (HAXPES) measures the energies of electrons that X-rays knock out of a material, which reveal the elements present, their chemical state and the electronic structure; with hard, high-energy X-rays the electrons escape from deeper, so buried layers can be read. At 28-ID-E a separate 'twisted' monochromator supplies 10 keV for HAXPES alongside pulsed laser deposition and surface diffraction. A published system of the same kind (Eres et al. 2019) worked at 4–12 keV with a Scienta EW4000 analyser, linking electronic and atomic structure while oxide heterostructures grew.

scienceCases.title: Crystals with a memory: island patterns during layer-by-layer growth
scienceCases.text: When gallium nitride grows one atomic layer at a time, small islands form on each new layer. Speckle 'movies' recorded during growth showed that each layer's islands tend to appear where the previous layer's islands were: the crystal remembers. Ju and colleagues (2019) grew gallium nitride by metal-organic vapour-phase epitaxy and compared the speckle at every pair of moments (two-time correlations), measured just off the anti-Bragg point midway between two diffraction peaks, where the signal is most sensitive to the surface. They traced the memory to surface atoms (adatoms) moving between layers, governed by the extra energy barrier they meet at step edges (the Ehrlich–Schwoebel barrier). That work needed a 'pink' beam with no monochromator, at 25.75 keV, and 10-second frames; CHEX's growth reactor in hutch F is designed to extend it with far more coherent flux.

scienceCases.title: Oxide films that rearrange their own layers
scienceCases.text: Researchers trying to stack oxide layers in a chosen order found, by watching with X-rays during growth, that the layers swap places on their own, and used the effect to make a crystal never grown before. Lee and colleagues (2014) used in situ X-ray scattering at APS 33-ID-E to follow layered Ruddlesden–Popper oxides growing by molecular-beam epitaxy, in which beams of evaporated atoms build a film in ultra-high vacuum. They went on to synthesise the first single-crystal films of La₃Ni₂O₇. The oxide-growth programme now has a station at 28-ID-C on the tunable branch, where resonant contrast, from tuning the energy to an element's absorption edge, helps tell the metal ions apart.

scienceCases.title: Following electrons and oxygen vacancies while oxide heterostructures grow
scienceCases.text: A laser builds oxide films puff by puff while X-rays measure both where the atoms go and what the electrons are doing, which matters for 'dead layers' that spoil thin-film electronics. Eres and colleagues (2019) combined pulsed laser deposition, real-time surface diffraction and in situ hard X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (4–12 keV). They showed missing oxygen atoms (oxygen vacancies) switching La_{2/3}Sr_{1/3}MnO₃, capped with oxygen-deficient SrTiO_{3−δ}, between two crystal structures, perovskite and brownmillerite. Station 28-ID-E hosts this kind of laser-deposition diffractometer, with a 10 keV 'twisted' monochromator for the photoelectron measurements.

scienceCases.title: Growing better qubit crystals
scienceCases.text: Silicon carbide can host quantum bits (qubits), but it is hard to grow perfectly. CHEX lets scientists look inside the growth environment as the crystal forms: the APS highlights in situ studies of silicon-carbide growth for qubit hosts, and the 2021 CHEX workshops covered silicon carbide alongside metal-organic chemical vapour deposition, atomic layer deposition and catalysts.

scienceCases.title: Chips: watching deposition and etching
scienceCases.text: Computer chips are made by depositing and etching films a few atoms thick. The APS strategic plan for 2025–29 foresees CHEX watching those steps with surface scattering and speckle measurements, to follow how films crystallize, where defects form and how strain evolves during each fabrication step. Because high-energy X-rays pass through the walls of deposition and etching chambers, these steps can be followed while they happen rather than examined afterwards.

scienceCases.title: Batteries, fuel cells and electrochemistry under operating conditions
scienceCases.text: Coherent X-rays can image a single battery particle in 3D while it charges, revealing defects that move and strain that builds up. Ulvestad and colleagues (2015) used Bragg coherent diffraction imaging to follow dislocations, line defects in the crystal, moving inside LiNi₀.₅Mn₁.₅O₄ battery nanoparticles during operation; the CHEX design report cites this as a model. CHEX brings such measurements to 15–35 keV, the range listed for electrochemistry and catalysis, where beams pass through electrolyte and cell hardware to reach solid–solid, liquid–solid and vapour–solid interfaces.

scienceCases.title: Rocks, corrosion and materials in harsh environments
scienceCases.text: From carbon storage in rocks to rusting steel, many important reactions happen in messy, hidden places. The design report's science case proposes 35–60 keV coherent beams to image, at the nanoscale and as they happen, mineral–fluid reactions in porous rock, corrosion (whose cost it puts at more than 3% of US GDP) and nuclear materials under load. An environmental load frame and a combined interface-microscopy and coherent-imaging instrument were proposed for this work.

components.name: Upstream undulator (as-built interim): 2.8 cm hybrid permanent-magnet undulator 'APS28#11S'
components.distanceNote: Approx: canted-pair ID centres sit ≈1.23 m either side of the straight-section centre (FDR Fig. 3.11: -1229.5/+1234.5 mm for 2.1 m canted HPMUs); FDR Table 4.4 gives ±1.25 m for the planned SCUs.
components.text: The X-ray source for the tunable branch: a 2.07 m row of alternating magnets that makes the ring's 6 GeV electrons slalom and shine an intense, narrow X-ray beam. Today it is an interim permanent-magnet undulator with a 28 mm period, the repeat length of its magnet pattern. At its 8.5 mm minimum gap its fundamental, the lowest of its emission peaks, lies near 3 keV; opening the gap raises it, and higher energies come from odd harmonics, overtones at 3, 5, 7… times the fundamental. A superconducting undulator with an 18.5 mm period is planned to replace it in 2026–2027. That this upstream device feeds the tunable branch is inferred from the APS canting convention and the design's heat-load tables.

specs.plannedReplacement: SCU, 18.5 mm period, 1.3 m (FDR Table 4.4); planned 2026–2027

components.name: Canting magnets (0.5 mrad + 1 mrad + 0.5 mrad)
components.distanceNote: Approx: end magnets at each end of the ≈5.4 m straight, 1 mrad magnet at its centre (FDR 3-3.3.5)
components.text: Three small steering magnets put a 1 milliradian (mrad) kink, about 0.06°, in the electron path between the two undulators, so one straight section of the ring feeds two independent X-ray beams. The beams drift apart by 1 mm for every metre travelled: about 28 mm at the first crystals and 65 mm at station B. A 1 mrad magnet sits between the undulators and 0.5 mrad magnets at either end of the straight; with the planned superconducting pair, the centre magnet will sit inside the shared cryostat.

specs.beam separation: ≈28 mm at 28 m, ≈65 mm at 64.5 m

components.name: Downstream undulator (as-built interim): 3.0 cm hybrid permanent-magnet undulator 'APS30#6S'
components.distanceNote: Approx: see us-undulator.
components.text: The second interim permanent-magnet undulator, 2.07 m long with a 30 mm period, feeds the three fixed-energy branches. Its fundamental, the lowest of its emission peaks, is set near 5 keV, so its odd harmonics fall at 15, 25 and 35 keV (3rd, 5th, 7th) and at 75 and 105 keV (15th, 21st). Each thin crystal downstream picks one of these off the shared beam and lets the rest pass on. A superconducting undulator with an 18.5 mm period, whose fundamental is 5.1 keV at full field, is planned to replace it.

components.name: Front-end GRID X-ray beam position monitor (XBPM1)
components.distanceNote: Approx: FDR Table 3.9 quotes the CUFE upstream mask (XBPM1 location) at 19.4 m; not given specifically for 28-ID.
components.text: A beam-position monitor inside the accelerator tunnel that tracks where each X-ray beam points, so the electron orbit can be steered to hold the beams still. It is a GRID monitor, which senses the fluorescence the beam excites in metal surfaces at grazing incidence. It must resolve slow drifts to 12 µm horizontally and 10 µm vertically, and faster motion (0.01 Hz to 1 kHz) to 3.7 and 2.4 µm. A second monitor (XBPM2) is built into the exit mask.

components.name: Front-end photon shutter (PS2) and safety shutters (SS1/SS2)
components.distanceNote: Approx: order from FDR Fig. 3.4 (upstream of the shield wall); 28-ID positions not published – value estimated.
components.text: Heavy shutters inside the tunnel that stop the X-ray beam and the stray radiation travelling with it, so people can safely enter the hutches downstream: a photon shutter (PS2) and two safety shutters (SS1 and SS2). They belong to the standard canted-undulator front end of the upgraded APS, rated for two beams of up to 10 kW each and 280 kW per square milliradian at their centres. Their exact positions at 28-ID are not published.

specs.CUFE sequence (FDR Fig. 3.4): clearing magnet / LPPS / SRV → BTFM1 → FM2 → lead collimator → FM3 → GRID-XBPM → PS2/IM1 → SS1 & SS2 → wall collimator → FEV → exit mask/XBPM2 → exit collimator → BIV

components.name: Storage-ring shield (ratchet) wall with wall collimator
components.distanceNote: Approx: hatched shield block spans ≈22.1–23.6 m on the 2025 ray-trace plan (MEDSI 2025 Fig. 2), measured from its 5 m scale.
components.text: The thick concrete-and-lead shielding wall around the accelerator tunnel, called the ratchet wall. The X-ray beams leave through a collimator, a small opening in a heavy block, and enter the first optics hutch, 28-ID-A; everything else stays inside. The front end that crosses the wall is windowless, which the 2025 as-built ray trace confirms.

components.name: Front-end exit mask with XBPM2 (two apertures, 1 mrad apart)
components.distanceNote: Exact for 28-ID per FDR Table 4.6 (25.6 m); FDR Table 4.4 footnote places the 2 × 1 mm mask at 25.4 m.
components.text: A water-cooled copper block with two small openings, one for each undulator beam, that passes only the bright central core and absorbs the hot outer part of each X-ray fan. CHEX asked for openings of 2 × 1 mm (horizontal × vertical) instead of the standard 2 × 2 mm; one design table still lists the standard size. There is no exit window: differential pumping keeps the ring's vacuum separate, which preserves the beam's coherence. A second beam-position monitor (XBPM2) is built in.

components.name: Front-end exit collimator (tungsten)
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.6 (path length from centre of straight section)
components.text: A tungsten block with a 5 × 5 mm opening for each beam. It stops bremsstrahlung, the very-high-energy gamma rays made when stored electrons strike leftover gas in the ring, from travelling down the beamline with the X-rays. For the upgrade these openings were narrowed so that beamlines whose monochromators shift the beam only slightly can still keep the bremsstrahlung contained.

components.name: Canted-undulator white-beam slits 28ID-SL-1
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.6 (path length from centre of straight section)
components.text: Water-cooled jaws with tungsten edges that trim one canted beam while it is still 'white', carrying the undulator's full spectrum and power, before it reaches the crystals. Which of the two beams this pair (SL-1) and its neighbour (SL-2) trim is not stated for 28-ID; in the same design at sector 34, SL-1 acts on the inboard beam.

components.name: Canted-undulator white-beam slits 28ID-SL-2
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.6 (path length from centre of straight section)
components.text: The second set of water-cooled, tungsten-edged jaws, trimming the other beam of the canted pair before the optics. With one pair per beam, each undulator beam can be shaped on its own while it still carries the full white spectrum.

components.name: 2 mm graphite heat-load filter (inboard beam)
components.distanceNote: Position NOT given in the FDR – placed just upstream of the first SCM for modelling only.
components.text: A 2 mm sheet of graphite in the shared inboard beam. It absorbs low-energy X-rays that the thin diamond crystals downstream do not reflect but would soak up as heat: in the design, the heat load on the first 200 µm diamond falls from 68.7 W to 16.4 W, about four-fold, helping the crystal stay flat. The design does not give its position; the model places it just ahead of the first crystal.

components.name: Diamond single-crystal side-bounce monochromator for D/E (28ID-MN-2)
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.7 (path length along the D/E branch from straight-section centre); also Table 4.5.
components.text: The first of the thin crystals that share one beam: a diamond 100–200 µm thick that reflects only 15 keV X-rays, sending them 23° sideways (outboard, away from the ring) into the D/E branch, while the rest of the beam passes through to the crystals beyond. At this angle the diamond (111) reflection picks the undulator's 3rd harmonic, three times its 5 keV fundamental. The design calls for liquid-nitrogen cooling and a symmetric reflection that preserves the beam's collimation. Station E also receives 10 keV from a separate 'twisted' monochromator, whose design is unpublished.

components.name: Secondary collimator 28ID-SC-1 (after first SCM)
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.6 (path length from centre of straight section)
components.text: A shielding block just after the first diamond crystal. Small openings let the two main beams through, while the block stops stray radiation travelling with them from spreading along the beamline.

components.name: Mono-beam slits 28ID-SL-6
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.7 (path length along the D/E branch from straight-section centre)
components.text: Adjustable jaws that trim the freshly reflected 15 keV beam before its first lens stack. Passing only the central part of the beam, where the waves are most nearly in step, keeps the speckle contrast high at stations D and E.

components.name: CRL unit 1 for D and E (28ID-CR-4)
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.7 (path length along the D/E branch from straight-section centre)
components.text: The first half of the D/E zoom lens, still inside the optics hutch: compound refractive lenses (CRLs), tiny curved beryllium lenses that each bend X-rays only slightly, so many are stacked in a row. Up to 19 lenses can be used for station D and 10 for station E, each with a 50 µm tip radius. With a second stack near each sample, it forms a zoom that changes the spot size without moving the focus.

components.name: Beam visualization monitor 28ID-BD-3
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.7 (path length along the D/E branch from straight-section centre)
components.text: A screen and camera for checking where the 15 keV beam is. The screen glows where the X-rays strike it, so staff can see the invisible beam while aligning the D/E optics.

components.name: Monochromatic shutter 28ID-SH-2 (P8-20)
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.7 (path length along the D/E branch from straight-section centre)
components.text: The D/E branch's own shutter, built for the monochromatic (single-energy) beam. Closing it makes hutches D and E safe to enter without interrupting the other three branches.

components.name: Beam visualization monitor 28ID-BD-1
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.6 (path length from centre of straight section)
components.text: A fluorescent screen and camera that slide into the tunable beam, so staff can see where it is while aligning the optics. It sits just upstream of the tunable branch's monochromator.

components.name: Shielded pipe through A (28ID-ST-2)
components.distanceNote: Position not tabulated; spans from SH-2 to the A outboard wall (≈33.4 m path) – approx.
components.text: A shielded pipe that carries the 15 keV beam out through the optics hutch's side wall into hutch D. Bent 23° outboard by its diamond crystal, the D/E branch leaves 28-ID-A about 33 m along its path.

components.name: Mono-beam slits 28ID-SL-7
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.7 (path length along the D/E branch from straight-section centre)
components.text: Jaws that trim the 15 keV beam just before station D's second lens stack. Every CHEX station has the same trio within about 3 m of its sample: slits, a lens stack, and a window where the beamline vacuum ends.

components.name: Collimator 28ID-BC-1
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.6 (path length from centre of straight section)
components.text: A shielding collimator just ahead of the tunable branch's monochromator. Its heavy block stops stray radiation travelling with the beam, while a small opening lets the X-rays through.

components.name: CRL unit 2 for D (28ID-CR-5)
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.7 (path length along the D/E branch from straight-section centre)
components.text: The second half of station D's zoom lens, 1.5 m before the sample: up to 64 beryllium lenses with a 50 µm tip radius. Trading lenses between this stack and the first one changes the spot at 15 keV from about 1.5 × 0.5 µm to 6.4 × 2.2 µm (horizontal × vertical) without moving the focus. The design flux at D is 4.4–10 × 10¹² photons per second, calculated for the planned superconducting undulators.

components.name: Window 28ID-WN-3
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.7 (path length along the D/E branch from straight-section centre)
components.text: A thin window of diamond or beryllium, light materials that X-rays cross almost unhindered, that ends the beamline vacuum 1.2 m before station D's sample. From here the beam reaches the sample environment.

components.name: Horizontal high-heat-load double-crystal monochromator 28ID-MN-1
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.6 (path length from centre of straight section); also Table 4.5.
components.text: The tunable branch's monochromator: two silicon crystals that reflect only the X-ray energy matching their atomic spacing at the set angle (Bragg's law), so turning them tunes the energy. They reflect sideways, in the horizontal plane, which reduces the effect of vibration on the beam's brightness, and the beam leaves parallel to the incoming one, offset sideways by a few millimetres that stay fixed as the energy changes (a fixed-exit design). Liquid nitrogen cools them: with the planned superconducting undulator, the design heat load is 697 W. Sources disagree on the range: 5–60 keV in the design, 15–60 keV in a 2025 paper, 6–30 keV listed in 2026 with the Si(111) crystals. A second Si(311) pair and an optional multilayer monochromator are in the design; their as-built status is unknown.

components.name: 28-ID-D general-purpose Huber hexapod diffractometer
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.5 (station table)
components.text: A shared, general-purpose Huber hexapod diffractometer: a six-legged platform on a rotation stage that holds visiting teams' reaction cells, such as batteries, catalysts and heated gas cells, at precise angles to the beam. In the design, the zoom lenses give spots from about 1.5 × 0.5 µm to 6.4 × 2.2 µm here at 15 keV. When the rear hutch E is in use, the instrument retracts ('beam-pass' mode) so the beam travels on.

components.name: 28-ID-D detectors
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.5: 36.5–39.5 m (start of range)
components.text: Pixel-array detectors, fast X-ray cameras that record the speckle from the D sample, sit either on the diffractometer arm or on a long-distance positioner, 1–4 m from the sample. Farther away, each speckle spreads over more pixels, so finer speckle can be resolved.

components.name: Diamond single-crystal side-bounce monochromator for F (28ID-MN-3)
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.8 (path length along the F branch); also Table 4.5.
components.text: A second thin diamond crystal, 10 m further along the shared beam, that picks out 25 or 35 keV and sends it about 23° outboard to hutch F, while the rest passes on. Two diamond reflections do this at almost the same angle: (022) selects the undulator's 5th harmonic at 25 keV with a deflection 2θ = 22.68°, and (004) the 7th harmonic at 35 keV with 2θ = 22.91°. Switching energy therefore changes the deflection by only 0.23°.

components.name: Secondary collimator 28ID-SC-2 (after second SCM)
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.6 (path length from centre of straight section)
components.text: A second shielding block, just after the second diamond crystal, with openings for the beams that continue downstream. It stops stray radiation travelling straight on from spreading further along the beamline.

components.name: Mono-beam slits 28ID-SL-9
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.8 (path length along the F branch)
components.text: Adjustable jaws that trim the freshly reflected 25 or 35 keV beam before branch F's first lens stack, passing only its most coherent central part. A smaller opening raises the speckle contrast at the cost of flux.

components.name: Moveable mono beam stop 28ID-BS-3 (end of D, manual)
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.7 (path length along the D/E branch from straight-section centre)
components.text: A beam stop, moved by hand, at the end of hutch D. When it is in place, the 15 keV beam ends here, so people can safely work in hutch E while station D runs.

components.name: CRL unit 1 for F (28ID-CR-7)
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.8 (path length along the F branch)
components.text: The first half of branch F's zoom lens, still inside the optics hutch: a stack of beryllium compound refractive lenses (CRLs), each bending X-rays only slightly, with a 50 µm tip radius. Up to 19 lenses are used for position F/1 and 12 for F/2; a second stack near each sample completes the zoom.

components.name: Beam visualization monitor 28ID-BD-4
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.8 (path length along the F branch)
components.text: A screen and camera for checking where the F beam is. It sits just after the branch's first lens stack, so staff can align the 25 or 35 keV beam after its crystal and lenses.

components.name: Silicon single-crystal side-bounce monochromator for G (28ID-MN-4)
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.9 (path length along the G branch); also Table 4.5.
components.text: The last crystal on the shared beam: silicon, set to pick out very-high-energy X-rays, 75 or 105 keV, that cross thick samples and vessels, and to bend them about 5° inboard, toward the ring. Two silicon crystals provide the (022) and (004) reflections, which select the undulator's 15th and 21st harmonics of a 5 keV fundamental at almost the same deflection, 2θ ≈ 4.93–4.98°. The design range of this branch is 45–105 keV; 75 and 105 keV are the settings listed in 2026.

components.name: Monochromatic shutter 28ID-SH-3 (P8-20)
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.8 (path length along the F branch)
components.text: Hutch F's own shutter, built for the monochromatic (single-energy) beam. Closing it makes hutch F safe to enter while the other three branches keep running.

components.name: Mono-beam slits 28ID-SL-8
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.7 (path length along the D/E branch from straight-section centre)
components.text: Adjustable jaws that trim the 15 keV beam just before station E's second lens stack. They set how much of the beam, and how coherent a part of it, reaches the laser-deposition chamber 1.8 m downstream.

components.name: CRL unit 2 for E (28ID-CR-6)
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.7 (path length along the D/E branch from straight-section centre)
components.text: The second half of station E's zoom lens, 1.5 m before the laser-deposition chamber: up to 64 beryllium lenses with a 50 µm tip radius. Together with the first stack in the optics hutch, it sets the spot at E between about 1.3 × 0.5 µm and 15 × 5.3 µm (horizontal × vertical) at 15 keV.

components.name: Mono-beam slits 28ID-SL-12
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.9 (path length along the G branch)
components.text: Adjustable jaws that trim the very-high-energy G beam before its first lens stack, passing only its central core. They sit 1.3 m after the silicon crystal that picks out G's energy.

components.name: Window 28ID-WN-4
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.7 (path length along the D/E branch from straight-section centre)
components.text: A thin diamond or beryllium window that ends the beamline vacuum in front of station E. Both are made of light atoms, so 15 keV X-rays pass through almost unhindered.

components.name: Shielded pipe through A (28ID-ST-3)
components.distanceNote: Position not tabulated; from SH-3 to the A outboard wall (≈42.5 m path) – approx.
components.text: A shielded pipe that carries the F beam out through the optics hutch's side wall into hutch F. Bent about 23° outboard by its diamond crystal, the F branch leaves 28-ID-A roughly 42.5 m along its path.

components.name: CRL unit 1 for G (28ID-CR-10) – nickel lenses
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.9 (path length along the G branch)
components.text: The first half of branch G's zoom lens. Beryllium lenses barely bend X-rays at 75–105 keV, so the design gives G denser nickel lenses, which bend them more strongly; up to 19 serve position G/1 and 15 serve G/2, each with a 50 µm tip radius. Whether the nickel lenses were built as designed is not confirmed.

components.name: Beam visualization monitor 28ID-BD-5
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.9 (path length along the G branch)
components.text: A screen and camera for checking where the G beam is during alignment. It sits just after G's first lens stack, at 42.3 m along the G path.

components.name: Monochromatic shutter 28ID-SH-4 (P8-20)
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.9 (path length along the G branch)
components.text: Hutch G's own shutter, built for the monochromatic (single-energy) beam. Closing it makes the long G hutch safe to enter while the other branches keep running; the tunable beam crosses G inside its own shielded pipe.

components.name: 28-ID-E in situ pulsed-laser-deposition (PLD) diffractometer with HAXPES
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.5 (station table)
components.text: A pulsed-laser-deposition (PLD) chamber on a diffractometer: laser pulses strike a target and blast off puffs of material that settle on a substrate as an oxide film. X-rays follow each atomic layer as it forms, while hard X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (HAXPES), using 10 keV X-rays from a separate 'twisted' monochromator, measures the energies of electrons knocked out of the film to reveal its chemistry and electronic state. A published system of this kind, then at APS 33-ID-D, worked at 4–12 keV with a Scienta EW4000 analyser; that the same system moved to 28-ID-E is likely but not confirmed.

components.name: Shielded pipe through A (28ID-ST-4)
components.distanceNote: Position not tabulated – approx (A downstream wall ≈43.4 m)
components.text: A shielded pipe that carries the G beam out of the optics hutch toward hutch G. Between the two hutches it crosses a 2.6 m walk-through vestibule, together with the tunable branch's shielded pipe.

components.name: White-beam shielded transport 28ID-ST-1 (43.5–60.6 m)
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.6 (path length from centre of straight section) (start of 43.5–60.6 m run)
components.text: A lead-shielded pipe, 17 m long, that carries the tunable beam from the optics hutch straight through hutch G to stations B and C, right past the experiment running in G. Partway along it opens into a small shielded enclosure (SE-1) that houses the branch's first zoom lens and shutter.

components.name: Mono-beam slits 28ID-SL-10
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.8 (path length along the F branch)
components.text: Jaws that trim the F beam just before position F/1's second lens stack, 1.8 m ahead of the sample. They set how much of the beam's coherent core reaches the diffractometer.

components.name: 28-ID-E detectors
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.5: 44.0–47.5 m (start of range)
components.text: Area detectors that record the X-rays scattered by the film growing in the laser-deposition chamber. They can be placed about 1–4.5 m behind the sample.

components.name: CRL unit 2 for F position 1 (28ID-CR-8)
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.8 (path length along the F branch)
components.text: The second half of the zoom lens for position F/1: up to 63 beryllium lenses with a 50 µm tip radius, 1.5 m before the sample. With the first stack in the optics hutch, it sets the spot size at F/1 without moving the focus.

components.name: Window 28ID-WN-5
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.8 (path length along the F branch)
components.text: A thin diamond or beryllium window that ends the beamline vacuum 1.2 m before position F/1. Beyond it the beam reaches the sample environment.

components.name: 28-ID-F position 1: Huber hexapod diffractometer
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.5 (station table)
components.text: A shared, general-purpose Huber hexapod diffractometer at the front of hutch F, where teams mount their own cells and chambers. When the rear position F/2 is in use, it moves out of the way ('beam-pass' mode) so the beam reaches the growth reactor behind it. The directory lists a hexapod diffractometer and a growth chamber in F without saying which position hosts which; the model assumes the diffractometer is at F/1.

components.name: 28-ID-F/1 detectors
components.text: Pixel-array detectors that record speckle for position F/1, 1–3 m behind the sample. In beam-pass mode they move aside so the beam can reach position F/2.

components.name: Mono-beam slits 28ID-SL-11
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.8 (path length along the F branch)
components.text: Jaws that trim the F beam just before position F/2's second lens stack. They choose how much of the beam's coherent core goes on to position F/2, 1.8 m downstream.

components.name: Mono beam stop 28ID-BS-4 (end of E)
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.7 (path length along the D/E branch from straight-section centre)
components.text: The beam stop at the very end of the D/E branch, behind station E. It absorbs the 15 keV beam after it has passed the laser-deposition chamber and its detectors.

components.name: CRL unit 2 for F position 2 (28ID-CR-9)
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.8 (path length along the F branch)
components.text: The second half of the zoom lens for position F/2, 1.5 m before the growth reactor: up to 63 beryllium lenses with a 50 µm tip radius. With the first stack in the optics hutch, it sets the spot size on the growing crystal without moving the focus.

components.name: Window 28ID-WN-6
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.8 (path length along the F branch)
components.text: A thin diamond or beryllium window that ends the beamline vacuum before the growth reactor. The X-rays then cross the reactor's own quartz wall, which their high energy lets them penetrate.

components.name: Photon mask 28ID-PM-1
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.6 (path length from centre of straight section)
components.text: A metal aperture, the photon mask, inside the small shielded enclosure SE-1. It absorbs any part of the tunable beam that strays from its intended path, protecting the lenses and pipes downstream.

components.name: Collimator 28ID-BC-2
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.6 (path length from centre of straight section)
components.text: A collimator inside the mini-enclosure SE-1: a heavy block with a small opening that lets the X-ray beam through and stops stray radiation travelling along the tunable line. It sits just behind the photon mask.

components.name: Mono-beam slits 28ID-SL-13
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.9 (path length along the G branch)
components.text: Jaws that trim the G beam just before position G/1's second lens stack, 2.8 m ahead of the sample. They set how much of the beam's central core goes on.

components.name: 28-ID-F position 2: MOCVD (metal-organic chemical vapour deposition) growth chamber
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.5 (station table); assignment of MOCVD to F/2 is an assumption.
components.text: A hot, gas-filled quartz reactor of the kind used to make LEDs and power-electronics chips: metal-organic chemical vapour deposition (MOCVD) grows crystals such as gallium nitride from gases like ammonia and triethylgallium. The X-rays pass through the quartz wall to watch the crystal grow one atomic layer at a time, and the set-up must hold still to well under a micrometre so the speckle stays put. Its predecessor at APS 12-ID-D had a fused-quartz chamber 70 mm across with 2 mm walls, working from vacuum to 3.75 atmospheres above ambient. Placing it at F/2 is an assumption of the model.

specs.chamberWall: fused quartz 70 mm ID × 2 mm (predecessor instrument, Ju et al. 2017)
specs.precursors: NH₃, triethylgallium (GaN growth, Ju et al. 2019)

components.name: CRL unit 2 for G position 1 (28ID-CR-11) – nickel
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.9 (path length along the G branch)
components.text: The second half of the zoom lens for position G/1: up to 66 nickel lenses in the design, each with a 50 µm tip radius, 2.5 m before the sample. Nickel is chosen because it bends these very energetic X-rays more strongly than beryllium. The design flux at G/1 is 0.21–1.2 × 10¹¹ photons per second at 105 keV, calculated for the planned superconducting undulators.

components.name: Mono-beam conditioning slits 28ID-SL-3
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.6 (path length from centre of straight section)
components.text: Adjustable jaws that trim the tunable beam just before its first zoom lens, inside the mini-enclosure SE-1. By passing only the beam's most coherent central part, they set how coherent a beam the zoom optics accept, trading flux for speckle contrast.

components.name: Window 28ID-WN-7
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.9 (path length along the G branch)
components.text: A thin diamond or beryllium window that ends the beamline vacuum before position G/1. Both light materials let 75–105 keV X-rays through almost untouched.

components.name: Transfocator 1 for B and C (28ID-CR-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.6 (path length from centre of straight section)
components.text: The first half of the zoom lens for stations B and C: a transfocator, a vacuum box with 13 stacks of tiny beryllium lenses that flip in and out of the beam, so the number of lenses, and with it the focusing power, can be changed remotely. Stacks of 1 to 16 lenses with tip radii from 100 to 1,000 µm allow fine steps, and a few one-dimensional lenses focus in one direction only. Up to 47 lenses are used for B and 35 for C. It sits in its own shielded mini-enclosure (SE-1), so lenses can be changed without disturbing the fixed-energy branches.

components.name: 28-ID-F/2 detectors
components.text: Pixel-array detectors that record speckle 1–4 m behind the growth reactor at position F/2. From farther away each speckle covers more pixels, which helps resolve the fine speckle from a growing crystal surface.

components.name: Shutter 28ID-SH-1 (P4-40)
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.6 (path length from centre of straight section)
components.text: The tunable branch's own shutter (type P4-40), inside the mini-enclosure SE-1. Teams at B and C can open and close their beam without affecting anyone else.

components.name: 28-ID-G position 1: Huber hexapod diffractometer
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.5 (station table)
components.text: A shared, general-purpose Huber hexapod diffractometer for very-high-energy X-rays (75 or 105 keV), which pass through thick samples, furnaces and reaction vessels. It serves surface, general and high-energy diffraction, and moves aside in beam-pass mode to feed the rear position G/2.

components.name: 28-ID-G/1 detectors
components.text: Area detectors 1–3 m behind the G/1 sample. At 75–105 keV most X-rays would pass through a thin silicon sensor unrecorded, so these detectors need dense, heavy-element sensors; the models used are not published.

components.name: Mono-beam slits 28ID-SL-14
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.9 (path length along the G branch)
components.text: Jaws that trim the G beam just before position G/2's second lens stack, 1.8 m ahead of the sample. They set how much of the beam's central core reaches the rear experiment.

components.name: Mono beam stop 28ID-BS-5 (end of F)
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.8 (path length along the F branch)
components.text: The beam stop at the end of the F branch, behind the growth reactor and its detectors. It absorbs whatever remains of the 25 or 35 keV beam.

components.name: CRL unit 2 for G position 2 (28ID-CR-12) – nickel
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.9 (path length along the G branch)
components.text: The second half of the zoom lens for position G/2: up to 107 nickel lenses in a row in the design, each with a 50 µm tip radius, 1.5 m before the sample. So many are needed because even nickel bends such energetic X-rays only slightly. In the design table, the spot at G/2 ranges from about 1.0 × 0.3 µm to 11 × 3.2 µm at 45 keV.

components.name: Window 28ID-WN-8
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.9 (path length along the G branch)
components.text: A thin diamond or beryllium window that ends the beamline vacuum before position G/2. Beyond it the beam travels the last 1.2 m to the sample.

components.name: 28-ID-G position 2 (rear instrument position)
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.5 (station table)
components.text: A second experiment position at the back of hutch G, kept free for large, long-running set-ups that teams bring with them; the design report's examples are bulk-crystal-growth systems and an environmental load frame. It receives the beam when the front instrument moves aside, and which instrument occupies it in 2026 is not specified.

components.name: 28-ID-G/2 detectors
components.text: Area detectors 1–4 m behind position G/2, at the far end of hutch G. Like those at G/1, they need dense, heavy-element sensors to stop 75–105 keV X-rays; the models are not published.

components.name: Mono beam stop 28ID-BS-6 (end of G)
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.9 (path length along the G branch)
components.text: The beam stop at the end of the G branch, at 60.5 m. It absorbs the very-high-energy beam that remains after the G/2 sample.

components.name: Beam visualization monitor 28ID-BD-2
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.6 (path length from centre of straight section)
components.text: A screen and camera at the entrance of hutch B that show where the tunable beam is during alignment. The screen glows where the X-rays strike, so staff can see the invisible beam.

components.name: Mono-beam conditioning slits 28ID-SL-4
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.6 (path length from centre of straight section)
components.text: Jaws that clean up the tunable beam just before station B's second lens stack. They pass only the beam's most coherent central part, which keeps the speckle contrast high.

components.name: Transfocator 2 for B (28ID-CR-2)
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.6 (path length from centre of straight section)
components.text: The second half of station B's zoom lens, 1.5 m before the sample: a transfocator with 15 stacks of beryllium lenses that flip in and out, holding up to 180 lenses with a 50 µm tip radius. Working with the first stack 13 m upstream, it squeezes the beam to a spot anywhere from about 9.8 × 3.4 µm down to 0.9 × 0.3 µm (horizontal × vertical) at 15 keV, without moving the focus; larger spots pass more of the beam. One-dimensional lenses correct astigmatism, unequal focusing in the two directions, and the slight distortion that heat causes in the optics upstream. The design tables disagree slightly: the listed stacks add up to 191 lenses, against a stated maximum of 180.

specs.1D lens stacks: R = 50 µm (1, 2, 4), astigmatism and heat-bump correction
specs.table inconsistency: Table 4.11 stacks sum to 191 lenses vs 180 max in Table 4.12

components.name: Window 28ID-WN-1
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.6 (path length from centre of straight section)
components.text: A thin diamond or beryllium window that ends the beamline vacuum 1.2 m before station B's sample. Both are made of light atoms, so the X-rays pass through almost unhindered.

components.name: 28-ID-B shared hexapod diffractometer
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.5 (station table)
components.text: Station B's shared diffractometer: a precision six-legged platform (a hexapod) on a large rotation stage that holds samples or small reaction cells and turns them to exactly the right angles, while detectors on an arm 1–2 m away or on a long-distance positioner up to 4 m away catch the scattered X-rays. In the design, the tunable beam reaches it in spots from about 0.9 × 0.3 µm to 9.8 × 3.4 µm at 15 keV. The design flux, calculated for the planned superconducting undulators, is 6.8–37 × 10¹² photons per second at 15 keV and 4.2–11 × 10¹² at 60 keV; flux with today's interim undulators is not published.

components.name: 28-ID-B pixel-array detectors (arm and LDDP)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.5 gives detector range 65.5–68.5 m; value is the start of the range.
components.text: Pixel-array detectors that record speckle patterns, either on the diffractometer arm 1–2 m from the sample, for alignment, or on the long-distance positioner 2–4 m away, for imaging and speckle measurements. At those distances each speckle spreads over several pixels. The models are not published; the preliminary design envisioned photon-counting detectors with cadmium-telluride sensors and pixels of about 55 µm.

components.name: Moveable white-beam stop 28ID-BS-1 (end of B)
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.6 (path length from centre of straight section)
components.text: A motorised beam stop at the end of hutch B, rated for the full white beam. When it is closed, the beam ends here, so people can safely build or adjust a large growth chamber in hutch C while station B runs.

components.name: Mono-beam conditioning slits 28ID-SL-5
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.6 (path length from centre of straight section)
components.text: Jaws that clean up the tunable beam just before station C's second lens stack. Passing only the beam's coherent core keeps the speckle from the growing oxide film high in contrast.

components.name: Transfocator 2 for C (28ID-CR-3)
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.6 (path length from centre of straight section)
components.text: The second half of station C's zoom lens, 2 m before the growth chamber: a transfocator holding up to 136 beryllium lenses with a 50 µm tip radius. With the first stack, it sets the spot at C from about 1.1 × 0.4 µm to 14 × 4.7 µm (horizontal × vertical) at 15 keV.

components.name: Window 28ID-WN-2
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.6 (path length from centre of straight section)
components.text: A thin diamond or beryllium window that ends the beamline vacuum in front of the growth chamber. Beyond it, the X-rays enter the chamber through its own windows.

components.name: 28-ID-C oxide molecular-beam-epitaxy (MBE) chamber
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.5 (station table)
components.text: An ultra-clean vacuum chamber for oxide molecular-beam epitaxy (MBE), which grows crystals one atomic layer at a time from beams of evaporated atoms, with oxygen or ozone supplied to form the oxide. X-ray windows let the beam reach the film, and surface scattering follows each layer as it forms. On the tunable branch, the energy can be set near an element's absorption edge, where that element scatters differently, to tell the metal ions in an oxide apart. It is probably the APS oxide-MBE system formerly at 33-ID-E, though the move is not documented.

specs.technique: in situ surface X-ray scattering during oxide MBE
specs.lineage (inferred): APS in situ oxide MBE, formerly 33-ID-E

components.name: 28-ID-C detectors
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.5: 73.0–76.5 m (start of range)
components.text: Area detectors 1–4.5 m behind the growth chamber that record the X-rays scattered by the growing oxide film. Placed farther back they spread the speckle over more pixels; closer in, they catch a wider range of angles.

components.name: White-beam stop 28ID-BS-2 (end of C)
components.distanceNote: Exact, FDR Table 4.6 (path length from centre of straight section)
components.text: The final beam stop of the whole sector, 77.4 m from the source. Like the stop at the end of hutch B, it is built to absorb even the full-power white beam, since hutches B and C are rated for white or pink beam.

instruments.name: Shared CHEX endstation (hexapod diffractometer + LDDP)
instruments.text: The shared instrument at stations B, D, F and G: a hexapod, a six-legged platform that tilts and shifts its load by tiny, precise amounts, mounted on a large rotation stage beside a vertical detector tower. It carries heavy reaction chambers (the preliminary design asked for 50 kg) and must hold them steady to below a micrometre and a microradian. For alignment a detector rides the diffractometer arm 1–2 m from the sample; for imaging and speckle work a separate long-distance positioner, on air pads over a granite base, parks it 2–4 m away. A third set-up puts a zone-plate objective on the arm for interface microscopy. When a rear position is in use, every axis clears a beam pipe ('beam-pass' mode). The 2026 beamline directory lists general-purpose Huber hexapod diffractometers in D, F and G; B's maker is not stated.
sampleEnvironments: Compact CVD, ALD, sputtering and etching chambers (PDR).

instruments.name: Oxide MBE chamber
instruments.text: An ultra-clean vacuum chamber at 28-ID-C for oxide molecular-beam epitaxy (MBE), which grows crystals one atomic layer at a time from beams of evaporated atoms, with ozone or oxygen supplied to form the oxide. Its own goniometer, a precision rotation stage, sets the chamber's angle so X-rays entering through windows can follow each layer as it forms, and on the tunable branch the energy can be set at an element's absorption edge to tell the metal ions apart. It is probably the in situ oxide-growth system that ran at APS 33-ID-E, where Lee and colleagues watched oxide layers rearrange in 2014, though the move is inferred.
sampleEnvironments: Oxide MBE (ultra-high vacuum with ozone or oxygen).

instruments.name: PLD diffractometer with HAXPES
instruments.text: Pulsed laser deposition (PLD) grows an oxide film puff by puff: each laser pulse vaporises a little of a target in an oxygen background, and the material settles on a substrate. Surface X-ray diffraction follows the atomic layers in real time, while hard X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (HAXPES), fed with 10 keV X-rays by a separate 'twisted' monochromator, reads the film's chemistry and electronic state from the energies of electrons knocked out of it. A published predecessor at 33-ID-D combined the two, with HAXPES at 4–12 keV and a Scienta EW4000 analyser.

instruments.name: MOCVD growth chamber on hexapod diffractometer
instruments.text: A glowing quartz reactor, fed with ammonia and metal-organic gases, grows semiconductor crystals such as gallium nitride by metal-organic chemical vapour deposition (MOCVD); the 2026 beamline directory lists it in hutch F alongside a Huber hexapod diffractometer. Measuring speckle demands extreme steadiness: the predecessor at 12-ID-D kept the sample still to much less than the beam size and its detector to about 25 µm at more than 1 m, using a Huber diffractometer combined with a hexapod and separate near and far detector positioners. The predecessor's fused-quartz wall, 70 mm across and 2 mm thick, held anything from vacuum to 3.75 atmospheres above ambient.
detectors: Photon-counting pixel-array detectors (the predecessor used a 512 × 512, 55 µm GaAs LynX 1800).
sampleEnvironments: MOCVD with NH₃ and triethylgallium (GaN benchmark: growth in the ≈800 K range, anneal at 1,120 K; Ju et al. 2019).

instruments.name: High-energy hexapod diffractometer
instruments.text: A shared Huber hexapod diffractometer in hutch G for 75 or 105 keV X-rays, which pass through thick samples, furnaces and reaction vessels; it serves surface, general and high-energy diffraction. Behind it, position G/2 is kept for large partner instruments, such as the bulk-crystal-growth systems and environmental load frame named in the design report. Detectors here need dense, heavy-element sensors to stop such energetic X-rays.
sampleEnvironments: Furnaces, load frames and bulk-growth systems (proposed).

geometryNotes:
Plan view (FDR Fig. 4.2, confirmed by the 2025 as-built ray trace, MEDSI 2025): the straight-ahead axis carries the outboard canted beam (upstream undulator) through 28-ID-A (≈23.6–43.4 m), along a shielded transport on the outboard side of hutch G (43.5–60.6 m, with the mini-enclosure SE-1 at 48.2–52.2 m) and on into the tandem hutches B (≈60.7–69.5 m) and C (≈69.7–78.6 m).

The inboard beam (downstream undulator) runs 1 mrad inboard of it (lateral separation ≈1 mrad × distance: ≈28 mm at 28 m, ≈40 mm at 40 m) and is tapped by three side-bounce single-crystal monochromators inside A. D/E at 28.3 m and F at 38.3 m deflect it ≈23.2° outboard (away from the ring, toward the experiment-hall outer wall and the control rooms), so these two branches cross over the tunable beam within centimetres of their crystals and leave A through its outboard wall (at ≈33.4 m path length for D/E and ≈42.5 m for F, scaled from FDR Fig. 4.2); G at 40.2 m deflects ≈5° inboard (toward the ring) into the long G hutch alongside the tunable transport.

All tabulated distances are path lengths along each branch from the straight-section centre (the sources actually sit at ≈±1.23 m).

In this exhibit, the branches begin at: D/E (28.3 m, +23.2°), F (38.3 m, +23.0°), G (40.2 m, −5.0°), positive = outboard.

Hutches D and E (and F) are rotated ≈23° relative to the main axis; D/E is a tandem pair, while F and G are single long hutches with two instrument positions each (the front instruments retract in 'beam-pass' mode). Every station has a CRL2, slits and a window about 1.2–2.8 m upstream of its sample; the beamline vacuum ends at the window.

The tunable DCM is a horizontal fixed-exit design, so the tunable monochromatic beam is displaced sideways (a 2025 ray-trace note mentions shifting a photon mask 4–8 mm outboard for monochromatic mode; low-resolution reading). Beam height ≈1.4 m.

CHEX spreads over floor normally used by 28-BM/29-BM (there are no bending-magnet lines there) and the short neighbouring 27-ID (PDR). Control rooms and support: Control Rooms D, E, F and the Sample Prep Lab lie outboard of the D/E/F hutches; Control Rooms B (outboard) and G, C (inboard) flank the downstream hutches (FDR Fig. 4.2). Chemical-exhaust and gas-cabinet infrastructure serves hutches B–G (PDR).

Naming caution: the 2017 PDR used different station letters (fixed branches B/C, D, E; tunable F/G); this dossier uses the FDR and as-built names.

Before the upgrade, 28-ID was unoccupied (2017) and later hosted the IDEA optics-test beamline until the 2023 shutdown; the canted front end and the FOE 28-ID-A were built early (2018–2019).

As-built check (MEDSI 2025 Fig. 2 plan): the outlines of 28-ID-A, B and C agree with the FDR plan to ≈0.2 m, but hutch G was built shorter and narrower than drawn in 2019, with its upstream wall at ≈47.5 m instead of ≈44.9 m, its outboard wall hugging the ST-1 transport (≈0.45 m outboard of the tunable axis), its inboard wall ≈1.9–2.7 m inboard, and a ≈2.6 m double-door vestibule between A and G.

interactiveIdeas.title: One rainbow, four experiments: the harmonic multiplexer
interactiveIdeas.concept: A slider sets the undulator gap (fundamental E1, 2-8 keV) and shows the comb of harmonics n·E1. Three crystals sit in the beam at fixed angles (diamond at 2θ = 23.2°, silicon at 2θ = 5.0°); the visitor clicks a crystal to swap reflections (111/220/400). Each branch lights up only when a harmonic lands on its Bragg energy; at E1 ≈ 5 keV all three branches glow at once (15, 25/35, 75/105 keV) while the unused light passes through the diamonds to the next crystal.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Why CHEX can run several fixed-energy experiments off one undulator, and how a crystal acts like a colour filter.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: E[keV] = 12.398/λ[Å]; Bragg λ = 2d sinθ with d = a/√(h²+k²+l²), a(C) = 3.5668 Å, a(Si) = 5.4310 Å; harmonics E_n = n·E1 with E1[keV] = 0.9496·E_e²[GeV]/(λu[cm](1+K²/2)); C(111)@15 keV → 2θ = 23.15°, C(220)@25 keV → 22.68°, C(400)@35 keV → 22.91°, Si(220)@75 keV → 4.93°, Si(400)@105 keV → 4.98° (PDR Tables 6.10/6.13): (111)/(220)/(400) match harmonic ratios 3:5:7 only approximately, so show the ±0.5° mismatch; Si/diamond forbidden reflections (e.g. 200) carry no intensity; even harmonics weak on-axis; finite energy spread broadens high harmonics (n = 15-21).

interactiveIdeas.title: Speckle needs a tiny spot
interactiveIdeas.concept: Visitor adjusts X-ray energy, focal-spot size (via a zoom-lens knob) and detector distance; a simulated speckle pattern is rendered on a 55 µm pixel grid. When the spot is too big the speckles shrink below a pixel and wash out; the meter shows contrast β collapsing.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Why CHEX needs micron focusing, long hutches and small pixels - and why higher energy makes coherent imaging harder.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Speckle angular size ≈ λ/a; resolve when λR/a ≳ p: a_max = 0.886λR/p ≈ 20·R[m]/E[keV] µm for p = 55 µm (PDR); e.g. 35 keV, R = 4 m → a ≤ 2.3 µm; oversampling ≥2 for CDI; coherence length ξ ≈ λz/(2πσ) (Gaussian Schell; other conventions differ by π); coherent flux ∝ B·λ² ∝ E⁻² at fixed brightness.

interactiveIdeas.title: Grow a crystal, watch the clock
interactiveIdeas.concept: A 3-D surface where atoms rain down and islands nucleate, grow and coalesce layer by layer. Linked plots show the anti-Bragg CTR intensity oscillating once per monolayer, the diffuse-speckle pattern, and a two-time correlation map building up in real time; a toggle compares 'no memory' vs 'memory' island nucleation (Ju et al. 2019).
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: How X-rays count atomic layers and how coherent speckle reveals hidden correlations between successive layers.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Kinematic anti-Bragg amplitude for layer-by-layer growth: I ∝ |1 - 2θ|² for fractional coverage θ of the top layer (period = 1 ML); diffuse island scattering oscillates out of phase with the CTR, peaking at half-integer ML; two-time correlation as defined by Ju et al. 2019: C(t1,t2) = <ΔI(Q,t1)ΔI(Q,t2)> / <Ī(Q,t1)Ī(Q,t2)>, with ΔI = I - Ī and Ī the pixel-smoothed mean, so the diagonal equals the speckle contrast; C > 0, = 0, < 0 means correlated, uncorrelated, anti-correlated island arrangements, and persistent arrangements give a 'checkerboard' of off-diagonal correlations with a 1 ML period; GaN growth rate in the benchmark was ~1.25 × 10⁻³ ML/s, frames 10 s (Ju et al. 2019).

interactiveIdeas.title: The X-ray zoom lens
interactiveIdeas.concept: Two transfocator stacks (CRL1 far upstream, CRL2 1.5 m before the sample). The visitor flips lenses in and out of each stack; the focal spot on the sample zooms from ~10 µm to <1 µm while staying in the same plane. A second mode shows how lenses focus each harmonic at a different distance so a slit near the focus rejects unwanted harmonics.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: How refractive lenses focus X-rays, why many lenses are needed at high energy, and why G uses nickel instead of beryllium.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Thin-lens focal length f = R/(2Nδ) for N biconcave paraboloids of apex radius R; δ ≈ r_e λ² n_e/2π (Be: δ ≈ 1.5 × 10⁻⁶ at 15 keV, ≈ 2.8 × 10⁻⁷ at 35 keV; δ ∝ E⁻²); two-lens imaging of the source with magnification set by both stacks; absorption limits aperture (transmission falls with N); chromatic focusing gives harmonic rejection up to ~10⁵ with slits (PDR); FDR max lens counts: 180 Be for B, 107 Ni for G/2. Zoom trade-off (FDR Fig. 4.4, station B): adding upstream CRL1 lenses enlarges the focal spot (≈0.9 → 8 µm H at 35 keV) but raises transmission (≈0.2 → 0.64 at 35 keV, 0.84 at 15 keV) - the smallest spots cost flux.

interactiveIdeas.title: Old ring vs new ring: how much light is 'in step'?
interactiveIdeas.concept: Side-by-side phase-space ellipses (size × divergence) for the pre-upgrade and upgraded electron beams vs the diffraction-limited ellipse λ/4π at the chosen energy. A counter shows the coherent fraction and coherent flux as the visitor drags the energy from 5 to 100 keV.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: What emittance is, why shrinking it 70× matters most at high energy, and what 'diffraction-limited' means.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Per plane, coherent fraction ≈ (λ/4π)/(Σ·Σ') with Σ = √(σe² + σr²), Σ' = √(σe'² + σr'²), σr = √(2λL)/4π, σr' = √(λ/2L); APS-U flat beam σx 14.5 µm, σx' 2.75 µrad, σy 3.08 µm, σy' 1.29 µrad; old APS σx 280 µm, σx' 11.6 µrad, σy 10 µm, σy' 3.4 µrad; result ≈2% vs 0.01% at 25 keV; energy spread (σδ ≈ 0.14%) further reduces high-harmonic brightness - label as idealised.

interactiveIdeas.title: See-through reactor
interactiveIdeas.concept: A cut-away MOCVD reactor with 2 mm fused-quartz walls; the visitor picks an X-ray energy and sees transmitted total flux and coherent flux curves, finding the sweet spot.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Why in situ experiments need high-energy X-rays and why there is an optimum energy for coherent experiments.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Transmission T = exp(-μt) with 4 mm total quartz path (two walls); μ(E) from NIST XCOM/xraylib; multiply by source coherent flux (∝ B·λ²); Ju et al. 2017 (Fig. 2, comparing the then-current 12-ID-D undulator, 3.0 cm × 2.0 m, with projected APS-U sources) give optimum energies of ≈30 keV for total and ≈23 keV for coherent flux transmitted through the 4 mm of quartz.

funFacts: CHEX gets three experiments out of one undulator: two thin diamond crystals each reflect a different harmonic (15 keV, then 25 or 35 keV) and let the rest of the light pass through to the next crystal, and a final silicon crystal picks off 75 or 105 keV (PDR; APS Beamline Directory).

Two of its fixed-energy beams (D/E and F) are bent sideways by about 23 degrees by diamond crystals – enormous compared with the few-milliradian (a fraction of a degree) deflections of typical synchrotron mirrors, e.g. 4 mrad at 25-ID (PDR; Beamline Directory; FDR).
At 75–105 keV, beryllium lenses barely bend X-rays, so CHEX's G station focuses with lenses made of nickel (FDR Table 4.12).

Before the upgrade, scientists had to pull the monochromator out entirely and use a 'pink' beam – the undulator's whole harmonic peak, about 1% wide in energy – just to get enough coherent X-rays to watch GaN grow (Ju et al. 2019).

An APS-U-design canted front end was installed at 28-ID and tested with beam on the old ring in November 2018 – a project milestone more than four years before the upgrade dark period began (FDR Ch. 1 and Ch. 3).
In 2017 sector 28 was empty; before CHEX was built it hosted IDEA, a temporary beamline for testing the optics that would preserve the upgraded APS's coherence (PDR; APS News 2022).
CHEX currently runs on 'stand-in' permanent-magnet undulators; superconducting undulators cooled to 4.2 K are planned to replace them (APS ID table 2026; Strategic Plan 2025–29).

Two branches use tandem hutch pairs (B/C and D/E): a beam stop at the end of the front hutch lets teams build and tune a large growth chamber in the back hutch while another experiment runs in front. F and G instead have two positions in one long hutch, where the front instrument moves aside ('beam-pass' mode) to feed the rear one (FDR; PDR).
The design anticipated about 1 terabyte of data per day from each of the four simultaneous experiments (PDR).
The upgraded APS ring's measured emittance (45 pm·rad at 50 mA) beat the previous world record of 134 pm·rad (APS News 2024).

CHEX grew out of years of community workshops; a 2018 project listing named Robert Winarski and Brian Stephenson as its science leads, and today's beamline team (Matt Highland, Zhan Zhang, Hua Zhou, Hawoong Hong, Tomoya Kawaguchi) runs it within the APS Surface Scattering and Microdiffraction group (MEDSI 2018; APS feature page; XSD-SSM).
Superconducting undulators are expected to give about three times the brightness of the interim permanent-magnet undulators above 50 keV (APS Strategic Plan 2025–29).
